items.title: Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux
items.summary:
The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load.

Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs.

To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko, an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year.

In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild.

Reviewing code is hard

Reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code.

To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative:

  1. LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence.
  2. LLMs are easier to bias. The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way.
  3. LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. No sane human can review the same patch applied to 100 slightly different branches to find the few that have incompatible changes.

How Sashiko reviews a patch

To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs, and requires each pass to record what it ruled out:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Gather context and plan\r\n -> Parallel specialist sessions (concerns + dismissed concerns)\r\n -> Triage\r\n -> Per-bug deep checks\r\n -> Review report'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2949a86d10>)])]>

Notes on each step:

  1. Gather context and plan: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity.

  2. Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion.

  3. Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it.

  4. Per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding.

  5. Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list.

All this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many important contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev. Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code.

What the data shows

The real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions.

It is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. In fact, LWN.net recently wrote that Sashiko has already become an important part of the kernel's development process and was the top bug reporter of issues in the 7.2 release cycle.

It prevents new bugs and uncovers old ones. When Sashiko flags a bug in a proposed patch, the author typically fixes it in the next revision before the change is ever merged. Many developers run Sashiko locally or in corporate private instances. The bugs that Sashiko helped to prevent leave no trace in the git commit log, making them hard to count directly. What can be counted are fixes for preexisting bugs that Sashiko finds and reports as a byproduct of reviewing new changes: Sashiko is cited in over 2000 mainline kernel commits and in over 500 of this year's official Linux kernel CVEs, spanning drivers, core kernel code, networking, GPUs, memory management, and virtualization.

Fewer bugs are slipping into mainline releases. Across the 18 kernel releases prior to Sashiko (Linux 6.2 through 6.19, covering 254000 commits), an average of 3.4% of merged commits required a follow-up fix within 60 days. Since Sashiko rolled out, that 60-day fix rate has fallen to 2.8% in Linux 7.1 and 2.2% in Linux 7.2, a 35% drop (with the 30-day fix rate falling from 2.3% to 1.4%). It’s too early to make strong claims, and obviously many other factors can influence release-to-release numbers, so we cannot solely credit Sashiko for the entire drop, but the trend is optimistic.

Since Sashiko was rolled out, the percentage of merged commits in the Linux kernel that received a follow-up fix in 60 days has dropped by 35%.

A clean review carries real signal. If Sashiko's warnings were mostly noise, commits merged with warnings would need follow-up fixes no more often than commits that passed cleanly. In practice, across 21,500 tracked mainline commits, patches that received a clean Sashiko review required a follow-up fix within 60 days just 0.9% of the time — less than a third of the historical baseline. Patches merged despite a critical Sashiko warning needed a fix 7.6% of the time — an 8x higher risk (and 6.3x higher even after adjusting for patch size). 

That gap is what makes Sashiko useful to maintainers: A clean pass instills real confidence, while a critical warning is a strong reason to take another look at the proposed patch.

This all tracks with what Linus Torvalds wrote in a mailing-list discussion a few weeks after Sashiko’s launch:

"As you say, Sashiko tends to be quite good. Even when it flags something unnecessarily and there's no actual problem, there's likely to be a reason for the question. And we've seen some truly stellar reports too. Things that are deep and subtle, and the AI is 100% correct. So anybody who thinks that all AI is slop is in denial about the current state." - Linus Torvalds (on lore.kernel.org)

What we learned from building and running Sashiko

First, benchmark-driven development beats intuition. While developing Sashiko, we tried many ideas that looked very reasonable on their face but didn’t end up working out. Other ideas were less obvious but worked surprisingly well. What was crucial: Early on, we built a benchmark out of nearly 1,000 real Linux kernel bugs and used it to evaluate every major Sashiko change. Every bug in this set was a real mistake that had passed human review by kernel experts, had been merged into mainline Linux, and later had to be fixed. On that benchmark, Sashiko with the new Gemini 4 Carbon model catches 75.8% of the bugs that human reviewers missed (using high thinking level).

Second, coding agents are not great at reviewing their own code. Models are trained to produce a working solution within a limited token budget. Asking these agents to review their own code might work well for isolated tasks, but for real, large codebases, creating a functional solution is often just 5-10% of the work. What’s really hard is to produce a solution that works all of the time, is well-integrated into the surrounding code, and doesn’t introduce subtle regressions. This is often substantially more complex and requires additional effort. Similar to human developers, agents benefit from external code review: Reviewers often spot issues that the initial author missed, even if they are not more experienced.

Third, open source and shared community ownership and development help to build trust. By being fully open and transparent from the beginning, Sashiko allowed anyone to run it the way they wanted: using different models (including open source and local models), customizing prompts, or even adopting Sashiko to other-than-Linux projects. This helped with community adoption and brought over 100 contributors to improve Sashiko, including some prominent kernel developers.

More and more engineers are putting local Sashiko instances into their coding-agent loops, so patches are checked against the community's review rules before a human maintainer ever sees them. We use the same workflow to build Sashiko itself ("Sashiko for Sashiko"), running it to review every change to its codebase and prompt pipeline both locally and through a Github integration.

Although Sashiko started in the Linux kernel, the need for an agentic trust layer applies across critical open-source software. Because the core review engine does not depend on C or on kernel-specific rules, the Linux kernel playbook (combining an open verification pipeline, community-owned domain guides, and a benchmark mined from historically known issues and fixes) can likely be applied to other foundational open-source projects such as GCC, LLVM, or Git.

"Now, I think the other side of AI - and this is where Sashiko comes in - is that it basically does end up being a tool that can then increase the trust in the patch. So AI giveth, and AI taketh away. But the basic issue shouldn't be AI per se, it should be that notion of 'trust'." - Linus Torvalds on LKML

You can check out Sashiko at sashiko.dev, or find the code on GitHub to run it in your own development workflow.

items.summary: LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce.

items.content_excerpt: Coding is the largest category of enterprise AI application spend, reaching $34B in 2026 . Every company now wants to know what all that spend returns, but most engineering leaders still can’t give an exact answer to what it's buying. To try to understand coding agent ROI, teams used to look at high-level data like usage analytics and AI consumption, but these don’t provide insight into what tokens actually produce. Answering the ROI question is hard and requires visibility into spend across users and teams, along with a way to connect it to outcomes. We felt this friction firsthand when spend with our own coding agent, Robin, started climbing, and is one of the reasons we built a model router. Now we're excited to offer a practical solution for our customers too. LangSmith now offers reporting built for coding agents, along with new capabilities that tie their spend to the pull requests they produce. This provides a clearer way to calculate the ROI behind coding agent budgets and understand how changes to models and policies impact it. The new LangSmith Agent Platform operates around the agent. Each agent has its own record and belongs to an "agent type" that determines what its dashboard shows, which data it connects to, and how it's evaluated. Coding agents are the first specialized agent type, and present data on pull requests, one of the signs that the agent's work is useful. LangSmith already traces coding agents across model providers, including Claude Code and Codex . With coding agents in LangSmith, the spend in each trace is automatically attributed to pull requests each agent contributed to. The attribution reflects the tasks a coding agent is used for. It covers both cases where a single thread can open several PRs, and where a PR can take several threads to finish, so data in LangSmith reflects what your agents actually accomplished and what it cost. Up until today, LangSmith enabled you to see the cost per trace for any of your coding agents, one trace at a time. This is useful for manual debugging, but doesn't provide visibility into trends across the entire team. The new coding agent overview page aggregates those costs and ties them to the pull requests your agents worked on. The dashboard shows KPIs at a glance, and clicking any metric opens its trend over time. For example, if your team switched models, you can compare before and after to see the impact of the change. items.content_excerpt: When looking to cut AI costs, teams often start with budgets or open-source models. But agent traces can reveal other opportunities to save. At Databricks, trace analysis surfaced several: offline replays showed no performance gain from upgrading from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, so we stayed on the cheaper 4.8; fixing common MCP errors recovered an estimated $1.2M in costs a year ; and traces showed that simple prompts were going to expensive models, prompting us to adopt Smart Routing . Today, we’re introducing Unity Gateway Insights , which automatically uses Genie to analyze millions of agent traces alongside your business data and ontology. It surfaces where tokens are being wasted: MCP errors that keep recurring, simple tasks running on expensive frontier models, and repeated workflows worth turning into shared skills, all in the context of your business and under the same governance as your other data. If you already have traffic flowing through Unity Gateway, open AI Gateway > Observability > Insights and generate a report for the last day, 7 days, or 30 days. Insights then writes a report on the tokenomics of your coding agent rollout that answers the following questions: You can add up to 10 questions of your own to a report, such as whether the newest model is worth it for your team's work. To dig further, continue the conversation with Genie. Ask which MCP server wasted the most tokens this month and who owns it, and you have a bug report ready to send. Finding this kind of waste requires a full record of every step of every agent session: inputs and outputs, tool calls, subagents, intermediate steps, latency, and token cost. A standalone gateway records only the requests that pass through it. Capturing the rest of each session means instrumenting every coding agent yourself, then exporting the traces to a data platform to analyze them. Pointing Claude Code at those traces still leaves you to design the investigation yourself, with no map of your business like the Genie Ontology provides. Insights runs the investigation we developed while rolling out coding agents to thousands of Databricks engineers. It samples sessions and groups them into workstreams by kind of work. Then it checks each workstream for failing MCP tools, bloated context, frontier models on simple tasks, and repeated workflows, and ranks what it finds by the tokens at stake. items.title: Keeping Agents Fast: High-Interactivity Decode with FlyDSL MonoKernels in vLLM
items.summary: How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:keeping agents fast high interactivity decode with flydsl monokernels in vllm
items.content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. items.title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
items.story_key: story|title:why your fine tuning job takes longer than the flops say
items.content_excerpt: Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs. A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models . The full version will be on arXiv soon. GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move. Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon. We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors. The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs. For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time: Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance. items.title: Regularized Score Centering
items.summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

items.title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.

items.content_excerpt: Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs. Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next. The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome. IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action. Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic. Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. items.title: Inference after coding agents
items.summary: Empirical research is changing rapidly as AI coding agents are becoming increasingly proficient in every step of it, from writing code to manipulating data. We argue that while the potential of coding agents for science is vast, their use in hypothesis testing poses a substantial threat to classical inference, as these agents enable a supercharged form of selective inference. In particular, we argue that coding agents carrying out empirical research introduce a new type of post-selection inference that combines human-like, open-ended search over an implicit space of estimators with programmatic replayability of both the selection and the estimation process. Indeed, we find that on simulated data with zero effects, four frontier agents report significant p-values between 54% and 98% of the time when asked to produce a compelling finding. We propose a simple procedure for detecting and correcting these distortions. After an agent has completed its analysis, we reset and replay it on subsamples of the data to estimate the agent's relative probability of selecting that analysis when it looks statistically favorable. For agents with stable selection behavior, the resulting corrected test is asymptotically valid and consistent conditional on selection. Importantly, the correction is learned from the black-box agent's actual choices rather than a model of how it searches, so it remains valid even as AI technology continues to evolve rapidly. In simulations, the correction robustly lowers the high false rejection rates to near the nominal 5%. We illustrate the method on applications from two published papers.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.323
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Code Mode, an experimental opt-in in which Claude writes JavaScript to call its tools; see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode to turn it on, or to turn it off for an organization
  • Added engines["claude-code"] to plugin.json: plugins outside their stated Claude Code version range are not installed, updated or loaded, and install and update pick the newest version that fits
  • Added type checking of a plugin's TypeScript hooks module to claude plugin validate; each finding is a warning, and --strict fails on it
  • Added to claude plugin validate the $ nouns a mod's engine.create hook adds, withholds or replaces
  • Added support for CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL in managed settings for Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Added an options menu (stop, switch to usage credits, upgrade) when a model needs usage credits that are turned off or used up
  • Added a progress heartbeat every 30 seconds while hooks run long in claude -p and SDK sessions, so a host such as Claude Desktop won't end the turn as hung (once it includes this version)
  • Added .docx support to Artifact tool asset uploads
  • Added a /diff to close hint to the diff panel, and the keys that focus and close a panel to the ? shortcut guide
  • Added a start-up warning for Bash allow rules with a * in a variable's value, such as Bash(PORT=* npm run dev)
  • Added a warning when a plugin's language server can't start, naming the server and what to check
  • Added a one-time startup notice naming CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE when Perforce settings are found and the mode is off
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES (available since 2.1.318): set it to 1 to turn off subagent progress summaries and the requests that write them (#86879)
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_HINT_COMMAND, which a program that starts Claude Code can set to have the exit hint name its own resume command
  • Added unsetOptionCount to the claude plugin install --json result: how many userConfig options are not yet set
  • Added isPromptCovered to the props a mod's pane is drawn with, telling it when a dialog or a field above the prompt covers the prompt
  • Fixed running /compact again, or after a command such as /context, summarizing away a message that Claude had not answered yet
  • Fixed a resumed session joining your next message to an old interrupted message that was not resumed
  • Fixed a memory spike at the next prompt after Claude changed a very large file
  • Fixed a setting saved in a running session undoing a hand edit made to settings.json moments earlier; a settings file you delete during a session now stays deleted
  • Fixed claude plugin commands and claude mcp list signing you out of a Console profile when they ended while the token was being renewed
  • Fixed Edit and Bash running out of memory on certain /proc files, and Edit hanging or running out of memory on devices and named pipes
  • Fixed Claude Code failing to start, or to clear stored credentials at sign-out, when saving its configuration file failed with "Out of memory"
  • Fixed requests sent without streaming failing on errors that streamed requests recover from, such as a rejected image, thinking block or beta header
  • Fixed ExitWorktree, the worktree exit dialog and /resume leaving the session in the wrong folder when the folder the shell was in before entering the worktree had been deleted
  • Fixed accents and other combining marks sometimes landing left of the text, leaving stale copies on screen, or silently disappearing when text wraps
  • Fixed the last key of a key chord, such as Enter in ctrl+x enter, acting on a dialog's text field when the chord's own action isn't available there
  • Fixed ps processes piling up when the process listing Claude Code runs before stopping a command takes too long
  • Fixed subagent transcripts and large tool results being saved apart from the session's transcript after entering a worktree created by a WorktreeCreate hook or belonging to a nested repository
  • Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile moving to another sign-in when /fork, the Left arrow or --bg continued it in the background; reopen any session that was open during the update
  • Fixed a background session sending a conversation under another sign-in when its named Anthropic profile is missing, changed or overridden; it now stops and says so
  • Fixed a session on an API key, auth token or workload identity from its shell (not a setup token) moving to another sign-in in the background; it now stops and says so
  • Fixed MCP tool calls ending in the sign-in server's error, such as TOKEN_EXPIRED, instead of asking you to sign in again
  • Fixed an expired claude.ai login showing "Credit balance too low" when a saved Console key or ant auth login profile without credit was used instead
  • Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile being handed to an older background service that could not keep its sign-in; it now says to restart the service
  • Fixed a background session's sign-in leaving the previous account's login or other credentials in place; it now clears them for every session on the computer, and a refused sign-in can leave no login
  • Fixed background sessions moving between a profile and the stored login when an update restarted them
  • Fixed sessions opened before a sign-in keeping signed-out feature flags after the sign-in
  • Fixed sessions that kept failing after a Claude apps gateway sign-in expired: once you sign in again with /login in another terminal, they carry on at the next message

  • Improved memory use with many subagents: a finished subagent's transcript is freed sooner instead of staying in memory while later subagents run
  • Improved installing with the install script: the latest version is no longer downloaded twice
  • Improved WebFetch speed and memory use on deeply nested pages
  • Improved the cleanupPeriodDays cleanup to count folders it can't read as errors
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's /v1/models to state max_input_tokens for models whose context window is certain on every upstream
  • Improved ToolSearch to say when a tool Claude searched for by its short name is already available, instead of only reporting no match

  • Improved the Fable limit message in -p, SDK, IDE and cloud sessions: it now says when the limit resets, along with how to continue

  • Changed sessions on other vendors' models with a smaller window: once full, they can fail every turn until /clear, so set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1 before they fill
  • Changed Claude Code's own ripgrep and most internal git commands to run without most of its sign-in tokens and API keys, so a credential helper or hook under such a git command no longer finds them
  • Changed MCP_SDK_GENERATION=v1 to run the v2 MCP client in a compatibility mode (earlier handshake, relaxed OAuth sign-in checks), because the v1 MCP client is removed
  • Changed the tool Claude uses to finish an MCP server sign-in so that it asks you to confirm, even in bypass and auto modes; where nobody can be asked, such as in dontAsk mode, use /mcp

  • Changed artifact updates to ask first, even under an allow rule, when people outside your organization can see the artifact or Claude can't check who can
  • Changed glab config set without --global or --host, and glab config edit --local, to fail read-only inside the Bash sandbox; run them outside it
  • Changed the Bash sandbox on macOS, Linux and WSL to ignore write access granted through a symlink in a writable folder that leads elsewhere or to a missing path; grant the real path instead
  • Changed "don't ask again" so an allow rule that looks like it holds a secret, or would be saved to a settings.local.json that git tracks, lasts for the session only and isn't saved
  • Changed the sandbox on macOS and Linux: git worktree add, move and remove now fail read-only, as do commits in a worktree the session wasn't started in or given, even one inside the project
  • Changed start-up to stop when a --settings file isn't valid JSON and has a sandbox key, even one that turns the sandbox off
  • Changed what happens when a tool's permission check fails with an error after a PreToolUse hook returned "allow": Claude Code now decides the call as if no hook had answered
  • Changed what happens when a tool's permission check fails on input that a PermissionRequest hook rewrote: Claude Code now asks again, or refuses the call where nobody can answer
  • Changed the GitLab merge request badge to show only for the repository a sandboxed session opened in
  • Changed the claude mcp add --help example to a local command
  • Changed mods: a *, namespace or negated hook on engine.create now only observes. To add or withhold a $ noun, hook engine.create by name
  • Changed claude plugin validate to fail a mod whose engine.create hook isn't written in the one accepted form; installed mods keep loading
  • Changed marketplace and plugin installs to fail when a git submodule isn't on the commit its repository records
  • Changed project (.mcp.json) MCP server approvals to match the server's exact name; an approval entry written in another spelling now asks again
  • Changed self-hosted runners under --trust-workspace false and VS Code sessions in an untrusted folder: the repository's settings can no longer disable your hooks or turn plugins on or off
  • Changed tool.list plugin hooks so the tools they add or remove apply to the model and every agent
  • Changed claude plugin install and /plugin to show a warning instead of success when a plugin's install command writes to stderr
  • Changed claude.ai chats and Cowork tasks to check a plugin file for secret keys before sending it, and to ask first if it may hold one
  • Changed claude rm and the agents view to say a session is removed from the list, not deleted; claude rm help says the conversation is kept and claude --resume lists it
  • Changed /stickers to say that the sticker pack is all claimed for now, instead of opening a page in the browser
  • Changed a managed settings policyHelper to no longer take environment variables from user or --settings files; set what it needs in managed env or the launching shell
  • Changed a /skill or @file typed between two files picked in claude.ai or the desktop app, or after a picked file and a link, to no longer take effect
  • Changed split-pane agent teammates to check that requests come from their team lead: one that outlives its lead has its asks refused, and plan approvals must be re-sent after /clear or /resume
  • Changed worktree creation to refuse checkouts whose .git folders are links or hold hard links, such as git-new-workdir layouts and cp -al copies; use a plain clone
  • Changed what Claude is told after safeguards stop a forked skill or a workflow agent: retry with a narrower prompt or tell you, instead of doing the work itself
  • Changed browser tool calls (Claude in Chrome, the desktop browser pane) to refuse some escaped or JSON-text inputs and tell Claude how to respell them
  • Changed workflows so that a prompt an app marks as not typed no longer reaches their agents as your request
  • Changed computer use on macOS to refuse key chords that hold Space with Control or Option, and more system shortcuts that need your grant
  • Changed first-run setup in Terminal.app to name the "Use Option as Meta key" setting, what Option stops typing, and how to undo it before you agree
  • Changed the maximum of CLAUDE_CODE_OVERLOADED_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_MS from 64000 to 300000
  • Changed workflows in the desktop app's Code tab to pause at a usage limit and continue after it resets
  • Changed the spend limit and 1M context errors, and /usage-credits, in cloud sessions and under Remote Control: they no longer give a web address

items.title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
